newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan budget aims to spur growth, curb deficit.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan budget aims to spur growth, curb deficit.

text.p: Pakistani Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz said on Friday his budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) aimed to reinvigorate the economy and boost exports, while keeping the fiscal deficit on a tight rein.
"We are now focusing on the revival of the economy," he told Reuters Financial Television in an interview just ahead of his budget speech to the National Assembly (lower house).
"These are our four critical targets: seven percent industrial growth, five percent agricultural growth, six percent GDP growth and 15 percent export growth," he said.
This year manufacturing grew an estimated 1.8 percent, agriculture 0.7 percent and gross domestic product 3.1 percent, while exports expanded 1.1 percent in the first nine months.
If Pakistan, mired in what Aziz called a virtual industrial crisis, could meet the targets set out in the budget, "the recovery phase will be over in the next few months".
At the same time, he promised to slash the budget deficit to five percent of GDP from 6.2 percent in 1996/97, saying this target had the approval of the International Monetary Fund.
He voiced confidence that the IMF, which has agreed to start talks in July on a new medium-term loan, would approve of the government's "home-grown" structural reform agenda.
The Fund had been concerned about whether Pakistan would pursue stabilisation measures with equal vigour. "This budget does fully incorporate those concerns," he said.
Aziz said Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's four-month-old government was determined to carry out structural reforms, rather than simply raising taxes to tackle the fiscal crisis.
A key element in the strategy was to "restructure those institutions that are causing an indirect fiscal haemorrhage" such as state-owned banks, utilities, railways and others.
The finance minister promised to overhaul the tax system because "higher tax rates do not mean higher collection unless the collecting machinery is reformed".
The budget, reinforcing tax cuts unveiled in March, had "withdrawn excessive taxation from many individual industries".
On the spending side, Aziz said debt servicing outlays were inevitable, but promised strict restraint in other areas.
"We have continued this policy for the next year to keep a very strong curb on the other expenditure and that includes defence expenditure," he said.

"The defence forces cooperated in view of the financial situation and reduced their current year's allocated budget by three or four percent. Otherwise the budget deficit this year would have been 80 billion (rupees) ($1.97 billion) and not 50 billion."
Aziz said inflation, running at 12.93 percent in May year on year, could be reduced to single figures in 1997/98 if production picked up and the money supply was restrained.
"We have also given full autonomy to the State (central) Bank to make monetary policy and fix targets beyond which the government should not be able to borrow from the banking sector.
"That will increase availability of credit for the private sector (and) also help to bring down the rate of inflation."
To reduce interest rates, now at 20 percent to 22 percent for most commercial borrowers, Aziz said he had reduced excise tax on bank loans, which would cut rates by 1.7 percent.

Aziz said he hoped to double liquid foreign exchange reserves to about $2 billion in 1997/98. "With the confidence of the business community returning, money is not flowing out any more, in fact it is coming back," he said.

Pakistan would have no problem in meeting its debt service obligations, but this ultimately hinged on exports. "If we achieve our 15 percent (export) growth target, then we are well on our way to financial viability in the medium run," he said.
He ruled out any immediate devaluation of the rupee, saying past devaluations had raised debt servicing and import costs, thereby fuelling inflation, without boosting exports.
"So I do not see any need for an exchange rate adjustment at the moment," he said.

Aziz said he hoped capital market reforms would increase foreign investment in Pakistan, adding that an IMF agreement, along with the government's stabilisation measures, could lead to an improvement in Pakistan's credit rating.

"We hope it will not be the government...but the individual enterprises that want to expand and invest, particularly the value-added export industries, that will be going out and borrowing in the capital markets to finance their projects."
